subChunks.title: Team Topologies, Conway's Law & Cognitive Load
subChunks.hookHtml: Conway's Law states that organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structure. This is not a suggestion — it is a documented empirical phenomenon. Understanding it means you can design team structures to produce the architectures you want, rather than discovering that your architecture has been shaped by your org chart.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Conway's Law

'Any organisation that designs a system will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organisation's communication structure.' — Melvin Conway, 1967.

Practical implication: if you have three teams building a single product, you will get a system with three layers or three components that match those team boundaries — whether or not that is the right architecture. The inverse: if you want a particular architecture, design your teams to match it.

The Inverse Conway Manoeuvre: deliberately structure your teams to produce the architecture you want. If you want two independent services, form two teams with clear ownership boundaries before extracting the services.

Team Topologies

Team Topologies (Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais) defines four team types:

  • Stream-aligned team: aligned to a flow of work delivering value (a product, a service, a user journey). The most common type. Self-sufficient for most of their work.
  • Enabling team: helps stream-aligned teams adopt new practices or overcome capability gaps. Temporary engagement, not permanent dependency. Research and education, not work delivery.
  • Complicated subsystem team: owns a complex component requiring deep specialist knowledge (payments, ML models, cryptography). Rare — most systems don't need this.
  • Platform team: provides a compelling internal service to stream-aligned teams. Reduces cognitive load; not a gatekeeper.

Three interaction modes: collaboration (working together closely — temporary), X-as-a-service (consuming a capability with minimal interaction), and facilitating (an enabling team helping).

Cognitive Load

Every team has a finite cognitive capacity — the total complexity they can hold in their heads and work with effectively. Systems that exceed a team's cognitive load produce slow delivery, bugs from misunderstood code, and engineer burnout.

Types of cognitive load: intrinsic (the inherent complexity of the domain), extraneous (accidental complexity from poor tooling, unclear processes, unnecessary dependencies), and germane (the useful work of building understanding).

Platform teams exist to reduce extraneous cognitive load. Team boundaries should be drawn to keep intrinsic cognitive load manageable — if a team owns too many services across too many domains, they cannot develop deep expertise in any of them.

Team Size and the Dunbar Number

Amazon's 'two-pizza team' rule (5–8 people) has a cognitive basis: communication overhead grows with n*(n-1)/2. A team of 5 has 10 communication paths; a team of 12 has 66. Team size also determines ownership granularity — a team of 5 can own approximately 2–3 services deeply. A team of 10 might own 4–5.

storyBeats.text: The Academy reorganised its five-team structure around business capabilities: one team for spells, one for users, one for tournaments. Within 18 months, the architecture had naturally separated along those exact lines — three services with clear API boundaries, matching the team structure. No architect had mandated the split. Conway's Law had done it automatically.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering VP Drea
storyBeats.text: Conway's Law is not a warning — it is a tool. If you decide you want a microservices architecture and then you think about teams, you're working backwards. Decide the team structure first, based on the domains you want to own independently. The architecture will emerge to match. Get the team structure right and you get the architecture as a side effect.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering VP Drea
storyBeats.text: Cognitive load is the constraint that team topologies optimises against. A team that owns too many disparate systems develops surface-level knowledge of each and deep knowledge of none. They spend all their time context-switching. They are slow and their reliability suffers. The right team boundary is the one that keeps cognitive load within what a team of 5-8 engineers can hold deeply.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering VP Drea
storyBeats.text: Enabling teams are one of the most underused patterns in engineering organisations. Instead of every stream team struggling independently to adopt a new observability tool, one enabling team embeds briefly with each stream team, teaches them the pattern, and moves on. A 4-person enabling team can uplift 10 stream teams in a quarter. That is a 40-person impact from 4 engineers.

learningObjectives: Explain Conway's Law and apply the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre to design teams for a desired architecture
Identify the four Team Topology types and classify a given team against them
Explain cognitive load types and use them to evaluate whether a team boundary is correctly drawn
Apply the Dunbar/two-pizza heuristic to team sizing and explain its communication overhead basis
commonMistakes: Designing architecture first and then teams — Conway's Law means teams should be designed to match the desired architecture, not the other way around
Creating large teams with ownership across many disparate domains — exceeds cognitive load, reduces quality
Platform teams that act as gatekeepers rather than service providers — creates bottlenecks and team resentment
Treating enabling teams as permanent support resources rather than temporary skill transfer engagements
assessmentCriteria: Can explain Conway's Law and give an example of it manifesting in a real system
Can classify each team in a 4-team org against the four Team Topology types and justify each classification
Can redesign a team boundary that is producing high cognitive load and explain why the new boundary reduces it
Can describe the three interaction modes and give an example of when each is appropriate
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Conway's Law to an engineering manager who is redesigning their team structure. Why does it matter? How can they use it deliberately? What is the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre? Give a concrete example.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
The Academy currently has the following teams:

  • Team Alpha (8 engineers): owns the spell service, user service, AND authentication — three domains with no overlap
  • Team Beta (12 engineers): owns the tournament platform, leaderboard, and payment processing
  • Team Gamma (3 engineers): helps teams with CI/CD setup, then disappears and leaves teams to maintain it
  • Team Delta (5 engineers): owns the shared database infrastructure and reviews all queries before they go to production

For each team: (1) identify the Team Topology type if possible, (2) identify what is wrong with the structure, (3) propose a correction.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Team Alpha (8 engineers, 3 domains):
   Type: attempted stream-aligned, but misaligned — three separate domains with different users and different rate of change.
   Problem: spell service, user service, and authentication are distinct domains. Authentication has different security requirements and change rate from spell management. Team's cognitive load is split three ways; expertise in each domain is shallow.
   Correction: split into two teams. Authentication team (3 engineers) — owns auth service + security concerns. Spell + User team (5 engineers) — owns spell and user domains (which are more coupled). Auth becomes an X-as-a-service capability for spell/user and all other teams.

Team Beta (12 engineers, 3 domains):
   Type: stream-aligned but oversized with domain mismatch — tournament and payments have fundamentally different compliance requirements.
   Problem: 12 engineers is too large (too many communication paths). Payment processing has PCI compliance concerns that should be isolated from tournament feature work. Large team develops shallow ownership.
   Correction: split into two focused teams. Tournament + Leaderboard team (7 engineers). Payment team (5 engineers) — dedicated to payment processing with appropriate compliance expertise. Both are stream-aligned but to different value streams.

Team Gamma (3 engineers, CI/CD):
   Type: attempted enabling team, but executed as consulting with no follow-through.
   Problem: an enabling team that disappears after teaching leaves teams without ongoing support. Teams revert to old habits. 'Helps then disappears' is not enabling — it is one-off training.
   Correction: run structured enabling engagements: embed with one team for 2 weeks, co-own the CI/CD migration, then hand over with documentation and a clear support model. Also invest in a Golden Path so teams don't need individual help — scale through self-service.

Team Delta (5 engineers, shared DB with query review gate):
   Type: complicated subsystem team behaving as a platform gatekeeper.
   Problem: reviewing all queries before production is a massive bottleneck — every team's delivery waits on Delta. Creates adversarial relationship and slows the whole organisation.
   Correction: transition to enabling + guardrail model. Delta's knowledge should be encoded into: query analysis tooling (automated EXPLAIN output review in CI), SQL linting rules, performance test harness, documentation. Teams self-serve. Delta facilitates the migration and provides consulting on the hardest queries — not approval for all queries.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: You are hiring for a new greenfield product at the Academy: a mobile-first learning experience with real-time collaboration, notifications, and payment integration. You have 20 engineers to staff. Using Team Topologies principles: (1) Define 4–5 teams with names, types, member count, and owned domains, (2) Specify the interaction modes between each pair of teams, (3) Explain how your team design follows the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre for the desired architecture, (4) Identify the cognitive load risk for each team and how you have mitigated it.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Team structure for mobile learning platform:

1. Teams:
   Learning Experience Team — Stream-aligned, 6 engineers
   Owns: learning content delivery, spell casting flow, progress tracking, mobile-first UX APIs
   
   Social & Collaboration Team — Stream-aligned, 5 engineers
   Owns: real-time features (WebSocket), multiplayer sessions, social graph, notifications
   
   Commerce Team — Stream-aligned, 4 engineers
   Owns: payment processing, subscriptions, invoicing, entitlement checks
   
   Platform Team — Platform, 3 engineers
   Owns: CI/CD Golden Path, service scaffolding, shared auth library, monitoring templates
   
   Mobile Enabling Team — Enabling, 2 engineers (temporary, 6-month charter)
   Helps stream teams adopt mobile-specific patterns (offline sync, push notifications, mobile CI)

2. Interaction modes:
   Learning Experience ↔ Social: collaboration mode initially (shared real-time session model); X-as-a-service once patterns stabilise
   Learning Experience ↔ Commerce: X-as-a-service (learning team checks entitlements via Commerce API; no co-development)
   All stream teams ↔ Platform: X-as-a-service (consume CI/CD, auth library, deployment tooling)
   Mobile Enabling ↔ all stream teams: facilitating (2-week engagements, then teams self-sufficient)

3. Inverse Conway Manoeuvre:
   The desired architecture has four independent services: learning, social/realtime, commerce, and platform infrastructure. The team structure mirrors this exactly. Conway's Law will produce service boundaries at team boundaries automatically. No architect needs to mandate the splits — the communication structure will create them.

4. Cognitive load:
   Learning Experience (6): owns learning + progress + UX APIs — related domain, consistent user type (learner). Risk: feature volume. Mitigation: platform team handles CI/deployment (extraneous load removed).
   Social (5): real-time is inherently complex (WebSocket, state synchronisation). Risk: intrinsic complexity of the domain. Mitigation: focused team, enabling team available for mobile push patterns.
   Commerce (4): payment compliance is a narrow, deep domain. Risk: PCI compliance knowledge gap. Mitigation: dedicated team builds expertise; smaller team reduces communication overhead on a compliance-sensitive system.
   Platform (3): owns internal tooling with 20-engineer customer base. Risk: being too small to serve all teams. Mitigation: invest in self-service tooling (Golden Paths) so teams don't require direct platform team involvement for routine work.

options: Software systems always grow to exceed their original design constraints
Organisations design systems whose structure mirrors their communication structure
The number of bugs increases linearly with team size
Two-way communication is faster than hierarchical communication
questions.correctAnswer: Organisations design systems whose structure mirrors their communication structure
questions.explanationHtml: Conway's Law (1967) observes that any organisation designing a system produces a design that mirrors its communication structure. If three teams must communicate extensively to ship a feature, the system will have three corresponding components. This is an empirical observation, not a criticism — the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre uses it as a tool: deliberately structure teams to match the architecture you want to produce.

questions.questionHtml: A team of 10 engineers owns 8 different services across 5 different business domains. They have frequent incidents and slow delivery. What is the most likely root cause in Team Topologies terms?
options: The team's cognitive load exceeds what 10 engineers can manage effectively across 5 domains
The team needs more CI/CD automation
The services need to be consolidated into a monolith
questions.correctAnswer: The team's cognitive load exceeds what 10 engineers can manage effectively across 5 domains
questions.explanationHtml: A team can only maintain deep knowledge of a limited set of domains. 8 services across 5 domains spread 10 engineers too thin — shallow knowledge of each domain, constant context-switching, and inability to develop expertise that prevents incidents. The solution is narrower ownership: fewer domains per team, better bounded by domain cohesion. The team should own 2–3 closely related services in 1–2 domains that they can know deeply.

questions.questionHtml: A platform team requires all teams to get approval before using any third-party library. What Team Topologies problem does this create?
options: The platform team is acting as a gatekeeper rather than a service provider — creating a bottleneck that increases extraneous cognitive load for stream-aligned teams
This is correct governance — all dependencies should be reviewed
The platform team is operating as a stream-aligned team
This reduces cognitive load by centralising decisions
questions.correctAnswer: The platform team is acting as a gatekeeper rather than a service provider — creating a bottleneck that increases extraneous cognitive load for stream-aligned teams
questions.explanationHtml: Platform teams should reduce friction for stream-aligned teams by providing compelling services that are easier to use than the alternatives. Acting as a gatekeeper (requiring approval) adds extraneous cognitive load — teams must navigate approvals instead of building. The correct platform team behaviour: maintain an approved library catalogue (guardrail), auto-scan for known vulnerabilities (automated guardrail), and provide a fast escalation path for non-catalogue libraries. Reserve approval for genuinely high-risk dependencies.
